what_it_does: Federated Learning (FL) is a way to train AI models across many devices (phones, hospital computers, etc.) without collecting their raw data in one place — each device trains locally and sends only model updates to a central server. Beyond the actual training step, FL systems also need to do a huge amount of bookkeeping work: scheduling which devices to include next round, detecting misbehaving participants, personalizing models, calculating who deserves payment for their contribution, and debugging. These non-training tasks turn out to dominate latency and cost (up to 98% of total time), because they constantly fetch large model snapshots from remote cloud storage. FLStore solves this by running these tasks inside the same memory that holds the data, eliminating the expensive round-trips.
method_in_detail:
The idea. In today's FL deployments the server fetches model weights from a cloud object store (like Amazon S3) every time it needs to run any analysis, and those network round-trips dwarf the actual computation — by 31x on average in the paper's measurements. The fix is to store the data in the same process that computes on it.

Serverless cache as unified plane. FLStore uses 'serverless functions' — on-demand cloud compute units (like AWS Lambda) that each carry their own RAM (up to 10 GB). Instead of separating compute and storage, FLStore treats each function's memory as a cache slot. A small model update (typical cross-device FL models average 161 MB) fits comfortably in one function's memory, so computation runs right where the data lives.

The Cache Engine. A central hash table maps (client ID, training round number) to the function ID where that client's model update is cached. When a non-training request arrives, the engine looks up which functions hold the needed data and routes the computation there directly, rather than fetching data to a separate server.

The Request Tracker. A second lightweight component tracks which functions are executing each request and whether they have finished, enabling parallel execution across multiple functions and result aggregation.

Four tailored caching policies. Because FL workloads are highly predictable and iterative, one-size-fits-all caching (LRU, FIFO) achieves 0% cache-hit rate in practice. SOLA instead derives four policies from a taxonomy of non-training workloads: P1 keeps the final aggregated model and per-client updates for inference/fine-tuning; P2 keeps all client updates for the current round plus pre-fetches the next round (for clustering, malicious-client filtering, contribution scoring — tasks that need every participant's update for one round then move on); P3 keeps one client's updates across consecutive rounds plus pre-fetches adjacent rounds (for debugging and reproducibility tasks that track a single participant over time); P4 caches recent hyperparameters and metadata for scheduling and tuning. The correct policy is selected automatically by classifying the incoming request type.

The result. Compared to an aggregator backed by AWS S3 object storage, FLStore cuts per-request average latency by 71% (up to 99.7% peak). Compared to an aggregator backed by ElastiCache in-memory cache, it cuts latency by 64.6% and cost by 98.83% — because ElastiCache still requires shipping data across the network to a separate compute server, while FLStore executes in place.
